Multiclass Weight of Evidence (WOE) Binary Problem with Simple Hypotheses Weight of Evidence (WOE) is a statistical technique widely used in credit scoring and other banking data science use cases. In the binary case, we compare two hypotheses (e.g. Default vs No Default) by calculating a likelihood ratio or log likelihood ratio (WOE). Using likelihood ratios and WOE, we can say how much evidence from our data increases or decreases the belief in the hypothesis (e.g., default), and when combined with prior odds (e.g., sample default rate) we obtain the probability of default (PD). In the example, we see that having 5+ days of delinquency increases the odds of default almost 5 times (WOE = +1.6). The problem is straightforward when we consider only two classes but quickly becomes non-trivial when we have more than two classes, yet the governing principle remains the same, as we show next. 1. Multiclass Weight of Evidence (WOE) Multiclass Problem Formulation with Simple Hypotheses Now imagine that we wanted to look at different types of default, Days Past Due (DPD) and Unlikely to Pay (UTP) through a similar lens1. In a multiclass setting, we can’t directly compare all three at once with a single ratio. Instead, we must choose a reference hypothesis and compute pairwise likelihood ratios against it. 1. This example will become part of a chapter dedicated to Logistic Regression with applications in Credit Risk. Multiclass Weight of Evidence (WOE) Multiclass Problem Formulation with Simple-vs-Composite Hypotheses Continuing our example with the types of default, Days Past Due (DPD) and Unlikely to Pay (UTP), we can use a different formulation to derive likelihood ratios and weights of evidence (WOE). Here, we are only interested in only one hypothesis, ignore the alternative (composite, e.g., not DPD). The key idea is that now we work with row sums to calculate LRs. This is based on the Odds form of the Bayes’ Theorem as formulated by I.J. Good1. 1. I.J. Good. Good Thinking: The Foundations of Probability and Its Applications. University of Minnesota Press, 1983. Good notes, the same odds-form Bayes formula applies whether the hypotheses are simple (a single, fully specified case) or composite (composed of multiple simple hypotheses). When we focus on one hypothesis H, the general formula derived from the Bayes’ Theorem gives us the essential quantity for inference, posterior odds O(H|E).Posterior odds Likelihood ratio Odds Odds

Multiclass Weight of Evidence (WOE) Wrap-Up Some open questions: • What is the connection between multiclass likelihood ratios / WOE and multinomial logistic regression? • How can we derive posterior class predictions using multiclass LR / WOE? • Can target encoding be viewed as a practical way to compute multiclass likelihood ratios?
